Money in families — everyone has history with it.
How to raise children — everyone thinks they know best.

questions.original: What is the difference between a healthy argument and an unhealthy one?
questions.paraphrased: What rules keep an argument fair?

vocab.definition: good for you; working well
treating someone as important and valued

possibleAnswers: Healthy fights the problem; unhealthy fights the person.
Rules: no insults, no old wounds, no audience.
Healthy arguments end with understanding, not just victory.

questions.original: What is something you have learned to apologise for, even when it is hard?
questions.paraphrased: What makes a good apology — and a bad one?

vocab.definition: to say sorry for something you did
telling the truth

possibleAnswers: I have learned to apologise for my tone, not just my words.
A good apology is specific; 'sorry you feel that way' is not one.
I apologise now for the effect, not just the intention.

questions.original: How do you handle it when someone is angry with you and you think they are wrong?
questions.paraphrased: What do you do first — defend, listen, or wait?

vocab.definition: to protect yourself or your opinion
to pay attention to what someone says

possibleAnswers: I listen first — their feeling is real even if the facts are not.
I say, 'I hear you,' before I say anything else.
I wait until the heat drops, then we talk.

questions.original: What is a conflict you are glad you walked away from?
questions.paraphrased: How did you know walking away was the right move?

vocab.definition: to leave a situation, especially a bad one
valuable enough for the effort or cost

possibleAnswers: An online argument — nothing was going to be gained.
A fight with a toxic friend — peace was worth more.
A work dispute where winning meant losing my dignity.

questions.original: What is a small thing that prevents many arguments before they start?
questions.paraphrased: What habits have you seen couples or friends use to avoid fights?

vocab.definition: to stop something from happening
something you do regularly without thinking

possibleAnswers: Asking instead of assuming.
Saying 'I need a minute' before it escalates.
Checking in: 'Is this a good time to talk?'

questions.original: How do you feel after a good resolution to a conflict?
questions.paraphrased: What does a resolved argument give you that an avoided one never could?

vocab.definition: the solution to a problem or argument
the happy feeling when something bad ends

possibleAnswers: Relief — like a weight I did not know I was carrying.
Closer than before. Honest conversations build trust.
Proud — we fixed it without breaking us.

questions.original: What is a conflict you witnessed that was handled beautifully?
questions.paraphrased: What did the people involved do that you admired?

vocab.definition: to respect and think highly of someone
calm and polite behaviour in a difficult situation

possibleAnswers: Two colleagues disagreed in a meeting and stayed friends after.
A couple argued in front of us — calmly, respectfully, then hugged.
Someone took a breath, said 'you first', and the fight dissolved.

questions.original: What is something you would never argue about, no matter what?
questions.paraphrased: Where is your line? What is simply not worth the fight?

vocab.definition: having enough value for something
to decide between things

possibleAnswers: Taste in music or films — live and let live.
How to fold a towel. There are bigger battles.
A stranger's opinion online. Not worth my peace.

questions.original: What advice would you give two friends who are arguing?
questions.paraphrased: What is the first thing you would tell them to do?

vocab.definition: an opinion or suggestion about what someone should do
to fix something that is broken

possibleAnswers: Remember you like each other. Start from there.
Talk about what you need, not what they did wrong.
The friendship is worth more than being right.

questions.original: What is something you love to complain about, even though it is minor?
questions.paraphrased: Why do we enjoy complaining about small things?

vocab.definition: to say you are unhappy about something
small and not very important

possibleAnswers: Slow Wi-Fi. Always. Even when it is fine.
People who walk slowly in the middle of the pavement.
The weather — it is a national sport where I am from.

questions.original: What is the best way to give someone criticism without hurting them?
questions.paraphrased: What is the difference between helpful feedback and a personal attack?

vocab.definition: saying what is wrong with something
opinions about how someone is doing

possibleAnswers: Start with what works, then what could change.
Criticise the behaviour, never the person.
Ask permission: 'Can I give you some feedback?'

questions.original: Have you ever received criticism that changed your life for the better?
questions.paraphrased: How did you know it was fair, even if it stung?

vocab.definition: reasonable and right
to make or become better

possibleAnswers: A boss told me I spoke too fast. It changed my whole career.
A friend said I interrupt. I worked on it and my friendships improved.
A teacher's harsh comment made me practise harder.

questions.original: What is the difference between complaining and asking for change?
questions.paraphrased: Which one actually solves problems, and why?

vocab.definition: a way of solving a problem
a polite ask for something

possibleAnswers: Complaining names the problem; asking proposes the fix.
A request gives the other person something they can do.
Both are valid — but only one changes anything.

questions.original: What is something you complained about that turned out to be your own fault?
questions.paraphrased: What did you learn from that moment?

vocab.definition: responsibility for a mistake
to suddenly understand something

possibleAnswers: I blamed the traffic, but I had simply left late.
I complained about a missed message, but I had silenced it.
I realised it was my own planning, not bad luck.

questions.original: How do you react when someone complains about you?
questions.paraphrased: What is your first instinct, and what do you do after?

vocab.definition: a natural feeling about what is right
feeling the need to protect yourself from criticism

possibleAnswers: My first instinct is defensive. I have learned to pause.
I ask for specifics so I can actually fix something.
I thank them — honest feedback is rare and valuable.

questions.original: What is a complaint you hear often at work or school that could be fixed easily?
questions.paraphrased: What stops people from fixing it?

vocab.definition: to repair or solve a problem
easy to see or understand

possibleAnswers: Meetings that could be emails. The fix is obvious.
Nobody reads the shared document — so update it.
Unclear instructions. One sentence would fix it.

questions.original: What is the most polite way to complain you have ever seen or used?
questions.paraphrased: What made it work so well?

vocab.definition: behaving in a kind and respectful way
working well and producing results

possibleAnswers: Starting with 'I might be wrong, but...' softens everything.
A friend once said 'I need your help with something' — brilliant.
Compliment first, then the issue, then thanks. It works.

questions.original: What is something people complain about that you actually do not mind?
questions.paraphrased: Why does it not bother you?

vocab.definition: to annoy or worry someone
able to wait calmly without getting angry

possibleAnswers: Queues — I use them as thinking time.
Bad weather — every season has its charm.
Being put on hold — I just enjoy the music.

questions.original: How do you know the difference between a real problem and a small annoyance?
questions.paraphrased: What question do you ask yourself to decide?

vocab.definition: something that slightly bothers you
to make a choice

possibleAnswers: Will this matter in a year? If not, it is an annoyance.
Can I fix it in five minutes? Then do it and move on.
Is anyone actually harmed? That separates the two.

questions.original: What is a complaint you are glad you made?
questions.paraphrased: What happened when you spoke up?

vocab.definition: to say your opinion or complaint
to become different

possibleAnswers: I complained about a faulty product and got a refund.
I spoke up about unfair treatment at work — things improved.
I told a friend something hurt me. Our friendship got stronger.

questions.original: What is the difference between a complainer and a problem-solver?
questions.paraphrased: Which one are you more of, honestly?

vocab.definition: a way of solving a problem
in a truthful way

possibleAnswers: A complainer stops at the problem; a solver brings options.
I am a solver at work and a complainer at home!
Anyone can complain; the skill is offering a way forward.

questions.original: What is something you would change about how people give feedback?
questions.paraphrased: What feedback style do you respond to best?

vocab.definition: opinions about how someone is doing
a particular way of doing things

possibleAnswers: Private, specific, and kind — that is the dream combo.
I respond best to directness with a smile.
Give it soon, not weeks later when it is cold.

questions.original: What is a kind way to tell someone their behaviour bothers you?
questions.paraphrased: What exact words would you use?

vocab.definition: the way a person acts
telling the truth

possibleAnswers: 'When you do X, I feel Y. Could we try Z?'
'I know you do not mean it, but it bothers me when...'
Focus on the behaviour, not the person: 'That action hurt.'

questions.original: What is a subject you loved at school, and what made it so good?
questions.paraphrased: Was it the subject itself or the teacher who made it alive?

vocab.definition: something you study at school, like maths or history
to make someone want to do something good

possibleAnswers: History — my teacher told it like stories.
Art, because it was the only hour without pressure.
Physical education — I got to move and laugh.

questions.original: What is something you learned in school that you still use every day?
questions.paraphrased: Was it from a lesson, a teacher, or the playground?

vocab.definition: helping you do something
an ability to do something well

possibleAnswers: Basic maths — I use it every time I shop.
Typing — from a class I nearly skipped.
How to work in a team — learned on the football pitch.

questions.original: What is a subject you hated at school that you understand now?
questions.paraphrased: What would you tell your younger self about it?

vocab.definition: to know what something means or how it works
to recognise the good qualities of something

possibleAnswers: Maths — I hated it until I realised it is a puzzle game.
Literature — I was too young for the books we read.
I would tell my younger self: it is not about the grades.

questions.original: If you could add one subject to every school in the world, what would it be?
questions.paraphrased: What would students learn in that class, and how would it help them?

vocab.definition: something you study at school
useful and related to real situations

possibleAnswers: Money — how to budget, save, and not be afraid of it.
Emotional intelligence — understanding your own feelings.
Cooking — the most practical skill there is.

questions.original: What makes a great teacher, in your experience?
questions.paraphrased: Who was the best teacher you ever had, and what did they do?

vocab.definition: a person who helps others learn
able to wait calmly without getting angry

possibleAnswers: Someone who believed in me before I believed in myself.
A teacher who made mistakes feel safe.
Patient, funny, and genuinely interested in us as people.

questions.original: What is a skill you wish school had taught you?
questions.paraphrased: How have you learned it since instead?

vocab.definition: an ability to do something well
to get new knowledge or skills

possibleAnswers: How to negotiate and ask for what you deserve.
How to learn — real study skills, not just memorising.
Public speaking. I learned it the hard way, at work.

questions.original: Do you think exams measure how smart someone is?
questions.paraphrased: What do exams measure well, and what do they miss?

vocab.definition: to find out the size or amount of something
the skill or power to do something

possibleAnswers: They measure memory under pressure, not real ability.
Exams miss creativity, kindness, and persistence.
They measure one day; life measures every day.

questions.original: What is something you taught yourself that school never covered?
questions.paraphrased: How did you go about learning it?

vocab.definition: learned by yourself, without a teacher
eager to know or learn new things

possibleAnswers: I taught myself video editing — YouTube did the rest.
Cooking — from my grandmother's old recipe book.
English! The best things I know came from curiosity, not class.

questions.original: What would your ideal school day look like?
questions.paraphrased: How would learning, breaks, and movement be arranged?

vocab.definition: perfect; the best possible
a situation where things are in the right amounts

possibleAnswers: Short lessons, long breaks, and learning outside sometimes.
Morning for thinking, afternoon for making things.
Choice — let students follow what excites them.

questions.original: What is a moment in your education you are proud of?
questions.paraphrased: What did it take to get there?

vocab.definition: feeling pleased about something you did
to succeed in doing or reaching something

possibleAnswers: Graduating — the first in my family to do it.
Passing a subject I had failed the year before.
Giving a presentation in a language that is not my own.

questions.original: How has education changed since you were at school?
questions.paraphrased: What change would you keep, and what would you bring back?

vocab.definition: machines and devices like computers and phones
to become different

possibleAnswers: Tablets and online learning — useful, but screens everywhere is a lot.
Teaching is more about understanding now, less about memorising.
I would bring back more outdoor time and play.

questions.original: What is a lesson from school that you only understood as an adult?
questions.paraphrased: What clicked for you years later?

vocab.definition: to suddenly understand something
knowledge or skill from doing something over time

possibleAnswers: That showing your work matters more than the answer.
That the 'boring' subjects were teaching me patience.
That school was about learning to learn, not the facts.

questions.original: What is one moment when you realised your English was actually working?
questions.paraphrased: What happened, and how did it feel?

vocab.definition: to suddenly understand something
sure of yourself and your abilities

possibleAnswers: When I understood a film without subtitles. Magic moment.
When I helped a tourist and they thanked me in English.
When I had my first full conversation without panicking.

questions.original: What is the hardest part of learning English for you?
questions.paraphrased: What makes that part tricky — and what helps you with it?

vocab.definition: not easy to do
the way you say words

possibleAnswers: Pronunciation — the same letters make different sounds.
Understanding fast native speakers.
Remembering which preposition goes where.

questions.original: What is your favourite English word, and why?
questions.paraphrased: What does it sound like, and when do you use it?

vocab.definition: the one you like most
the idea that a word expresses

possibleAnswers: 'Serendipity' — it sounds like a little gift.
'Bubbly' — it makes me smile every time.
I love short ones like 'home' — so much meaning in four letters.

questions.original: How do you practise English outside of lessons?
questions.paraphrased: What is your favourite hidden way of learning?

vocab.definition: to do something again to get better
to make or become better

possibleAnswers: Watching series with English subtitles.
Talking to myself in English — embarrassing but effective!
Reading about my hobbies in English instead of my language.

questions.original: What is a mistake in English that you will never make again?
questions.paraphrased: What happened that made it stick in your memory?

vocab.definition: something you do wrong
to keep something in your mind

possibleAnswers: I once said 'I am pregnant' instead of 'I am embarrassed'. Never again.
Confusing 'borrow' and 'lend' in front of a whole class.
A funny mix-up that everyone laughed at — now I never forget it.

questions.original: What do you think is the fastest way to improve English?
questions.paraphrased: What has actually worked for you or people you know?

vocab.definition: to make or become better
a way of doing something

possibleAnswers: Speaking every day, even badly — mistakes are the fast track.
Living the language: music, films, friends, all in English.
Consistency beats intensity — twenty minutes daily wins.

questions.original: What is a word you love saying in English just for the sound of it?
questions.paraphrased: What makes it satisfying to say?

vocab.definition: something you hear
giving you a good feeling

possibleAnswers: 'Absolutely' — it sounds so confident.
'Whisper' — it sounds like what it means.
'Splendid' — nobody uses it, which makes it fun.

questions.original: How has learning English changed your life?
questions.paraphrased: What opportunities or people has it brought you?

vocab.definition: a chance to do something good
to join or link with others

possibleAnswers: It opened my career — I work with international teams now.
I made friends from countries I could never visit.
I can enjoy books, films and music in their original language.

questions.original: What is something about English that still surprises you?
questions.paraphrased: What rule or quirk feels strange even now?

vocab.definition: to make someone feel unexpected wonder
unusual or surprising

possibleAnswers: That 'read' and 'read' are spelled the same but sound different.
That there is no rule — you just have to feel it.
How many words English stole from other languages!

questions.original: What advice would you give someone starting to learn English?
questions.paraphrased: What do you wish someone had told you at the start?

vocab.definition: an opinion or suggestion about what someone should do
able to wait calmly without getting angry

possibleAnswers: Do not wait until you are 'ready' — start speaking now.
Be patient; the progress is invisible until it suddenly is not.
Find English you love — a show, a singer — and let it teach you.

questions.original: What is your next English goal, and how will you reach it?
questions.paraphrased: What is the first small step this week?

vocab.definition: something you aim to achieve
to succeed in doing or reaching something

possibleAnswers: Hold a five-minute conversation without translating in my head.
Pass the B2 exam — with daily listening practice.
Watch a full film with no subtitles at all.

questions.original: What is one English expression you use that you are proud of?
questions.paraphrased: When did you first use it naturally, without thinking?

vocab.definition: a group of words with a special meaning
normal and relaxed, not forced

possibleAnswers: 'That's a fair point' — it sounds so diplomatic.
'I'm all ears' — it makes people smile.
Using 'by the way' naturally felt like a milestone.

questions.original: What is a kind of intelligence that school does not measure?
questions.paraphrased: Who do you know who has it, and how does it show?

vocab.definition: the ability to learn and understand
to find out the size or amount of something

possibleAnswers: Emotional intelligence — reading a room, calming a friend.
Practical intelligence — fixing things with your hands.
Social intelligence — making everyone feel included.

questions.original: What is something you are naturally good at?
questions.paraphrased: Did you always know, or did someone point it out?

vocab.definition: without trying hard; by nature
a natural ability to do something well

possibleAnswers: Explaining things — I can make complicated ideas simple.
Remembering faces and names.
Making people feel comfortable in new situations.

questions.original: What is a skill you had to work very hard to learn?
questions.paraphrased: What kept you going when it was difficult?

vocab.definition: the work you put into something
continuing even when it is hard

possibleAnswers: English — it took years of persistence, and it was worth it.
Driving — I failed the test twice before passing.
A musical instrument — my fingers hurt for months.

questions.original: Do you think intelligence is fixed at birth or something you can grow?
questions.paraphrased: What evidence from your own life supports your answer?

vocab.definition: to become bigger or better over time
facts that show something is true

possibleAnswers: It grows — I am smarter at forty than at twenty.
Both: some things come naturally, but effort grows everything.
I have seen people transform with practice. It is growable.

questions.original: What is the difference between being smart and being wise?
questions.paraphrased: Who is the wisest person you know, and what makes them wise?

vocab.definition: quick at learning and understanding
having good judgement based on experience

possibleAnswers: Smart answers questions; wise asks the right ones.
Smart knows facts; wise knows people.
My grandmother is wise — she rarely lectures, but is always right.

questions.original: What is a question you are curious about and would love to understand?
questions.paraphrased: How would you go about learning the answer?

vocab.definition: eager to know or learn new things
to find something for the first time

possibleAnswers: Why we dream — I would read neuroscience for that.
How languages change over time.
What makes some people resilient and others not.

questions.original: What is something you understand deeply that is hard to explain to others?
questions.paraphrased: How do you usually try to explain it?

vocab.definition: to make something clear to someone
difficult to understand or explain

possibleAnswers: How music makes me feel — words never do it justice.
The logic of my favourite video game's economy.
A feeling about people — my instinct for who to trust.

questions.original: What is a time you solved a problem creatively?
questions.paraphrased: What did everyone else try, and what did you do differently?

vocab.definition: using new or unusual ideas
a way of solving a problem

possibleAnswers: I fixed a work problem by asking the person who never spoke up.
I solved a packing disaster by rolling instead of folding.
I turned a boring presentation into a game — everyone remembered it.

questions.original: What is something you know more about than most people?
questions.paraphrased: How did you become an expert in that?

vocab.definition: someone with deep knowledge of a subject
the things you know

possibleAnswers: Coffee — I worked in a café for years and never stopped learning.
My hometown's history — I am a walking guide.
Music production — thousands of hours of happy obsession.

questions.original: What is a talent you wish you had?
questions.paraphrased: What would you do with it if you woke up with it tomorrow?

vocab.definition: a natural ability to do something well
to want something that is not true now

possibleAnswers: Perfect pitch — I would compose music all day.
Speaking five languages — the world would open up.
Drawing — I would illustrate the stories in my head.

questions.original: How do you learn best: reading, listening, doing, or talking?
questions.paraphrased: What is a learning style that never works for you?

vocab.definition: a way of doing something
working well and producing results

possibleAnswers: Doing — I only learn by trying and failing.
Listening — podcasts teach me faster than books.
Talking — I understand something once I explain it to someone.

questions.original: What is the smartest decision you have ever made?
questions.paraphrased: What made it the right call at the time?

vocab.definition: a choice you make after thinking
the act of deciding between options

possibleAnswers: Learning English — it changed everything for me.
Moving abroad when everyone said I was crazy.
Choosing my partner — best decision I have made.

questions.original: What does being 'intelligent' mean to you?
questions.paraphrased: How has your definition changed over the years?

vocab.definition: the meaning of a word or idea
treating someone as important and valued

possibleAnswers: It means learning fast AND being kind with what you know.
I used to think it was grades. Now I think it is curiosity.
Intelligence is knowing what you do not know.
